references.text: Moses exhorts the Israelites to lend willingly to their poor brother without calculating any return, which stands in contrast to lending only to those from whom one expects repayment.

The prohibition against taking interest from a poor brother in Israel. The law mandates generous lending without profit, serving as background for Jesus' teaching on lending without expecting anything back.

The preceding verses in the same passage pose similar rhetorical questions: If you love those who love you, or do good to those who do good to you – what thanks do you have? Verse 34 follows the same pattern regarding lending.
The following verse gives Jesus' summary and conclusion: Love your enemies, do good, and lend without expecting anything back. This is the positive counterpart to the rhetorical question in verse 34.
Matthew's parallel to Luke 6:32-34 where Jesus asks similar rhetorical questions about loving only those who love you – do not even tax collectors do the same?
Jesus' command to give to those who ask, and not turn away from those who want to borrow – a parallel to the theme of generous lending without expectation of repayment.
The promise that the Lord will bless Israel so that they can lend to many nations, yet need not borrow themselves – God's people are to be generous lenders.
The righteous person is always merciful and lends freely – a description of the godly one who gives and lends without demanding return.
It goes well with the one who is merciful and lends, and who manages their affairs with justice. The psalm describes the righteousness's generosity in lending as a sign of godliness.
Jesus' teaching on inviting those who cannot repay you, instead of friends and wealthy neighbors – the same principle of doing good without expectation of return.
